puzzles.title: A pair of stepping stones
puzzles.instruction: Cover both squares with one domino.
puzzles.idea: A domino makes one neighboring pair.
hints: Find the two squares.
They touch along a whole side.
Tap one square, then the other.

parent.notice: Notice whether your child uses touching sides rather than touching corners.
parent.prompt: What makes these two squares a pair?
parent.explanation: There are two squares and one allowed neighboring pair. Covering them gives a complete matching: every square has exactly one partner.
parent.extension: Draw two squares that touch only at a corner. Can one straight domino cover them?
parent.connection: A first example of a perfect matching.

puzzles.title: The narrow trail
puzzles.instruction: Cover the trail. Start at either end.
puzzles.idea: An end can tell us what must happen next.
hints: Look for an end of the trail.
That square has just one neighbor.
Pair the two left squares, then the two right squares.

parent.notice: Notice the move your child calls unavoidable.
parent.prompt: Could the end square choose a different partner?
parent.explanation: An end has only one neighbor, so its domino is forced. Removing that pair leaves another pair. The middle pair alone would strand both ends.
parent.extension: Draw a trail of six squares. Keep removing a pair from an end.
parent.connection: Forced choices are useful when constructing matchings.

puzzles.title: A square, two ways
puzzles.instruction: Cover the little square.
puzzles.idea: One shape can have more than one solution.
hints: A domino can lie across or stand up.
Try covering one whole row.
Cover the top row, then the bottom row.

parent.notice: A different solution is worth noticing even after the puzzle is finished.
parent.prompt: Can you cover the same square another way?
parent.explanation: The top-left square has two possible partners. Each choice forces the other domino. So there are exactly two tilings: two across or two upright.
parent.extension: Remove both dominoes and turn both. Mathematicians call this two-domino change a flip.
parent.connection: This is the smallest local move between tilings.

puzzles.title: Around the bend
puzzles.instruction: Cover the path around the bend.
puzzles.idea: A tricky shape may have an easy starting place.
hints: Find a square at a tip.
The bottom square can only reach upward.
Pair the left two squares up and down. Pair the two remaining top squares.

parent.notice: Watch for a switch between horizontal and vertical thinking.
parent.prompt: Which square helped you decide where to start?
parent.explanation: The bottom tip forces a vertical domino. The two remaining top squares then form a horizontal pair. This is the only complete tiling.
parent.extension: Turn a paper copy around. Does turning the whole board change its solution?
parent.connection: Local constraints can determine an entire matching.

puzzles.title: Three little steps
puzzles.instruction: Cover all three steps.
puzzles.idea: An even number is helpful, but neighbors still matter.
hints: Look at the top-left tip.
After its pair is covered, look for the next tip.
Place one domino across each short row.

parent.notice: Notice whether the child follows the trail of forced choices.
parent.prompt: Why can each step be a pair?
parent.explanation: Each row has two squares. Covering each row works. Starting from the top-left tip also proves that these three horizontal pairs are forced.
parent.extension: Add one more two-square step on paper. Explain how the old solution grows.
parent.connection: Building a larger example from a smaller one prepares for induction.

puzzles.title: Three across
puzzles.instruction: Cover the six-square garden.
puzzles.idea: Odd rows can help one another.
hints: Count the squares in one row.
A domino may reach from one row to the other.
Try three upright dominoes, one in each column.

parent.notice: A row of three need not be solved by itself.
parent.prompt: Where can the last square in a row find a partner?
parent.explanation: A horizontal-only attempt leaves one square in each row. A vertical domino can pair those leftovers. Three vertical dominoes also cover everything.
parent.extension: Find a tiling with just one upright domino. Then find one with three.
parent.connection: Choosing a useful boundary between subproblems matters.

puzzles.title: A room with a tail
puzzles.instruction: Cover the room and its little tail.
puzzles.idea: Solve a forced part, then a free part.
hints: Find the far-right tip.
The two tail squares can make a pair.
Cover the tail across. Then cover the little square that remains.

parent.notice: The tail has one choice; the square room has two.
parent.prompt: Which part can you change without touching the tail?
parent.explanation: The far-right square forces the tail domino. The remaining 2 by 2 room has two tilings. The tail stays the same in both.
parent.extension: Change just the room by turning its two dominoes together.
parent.connection: Separate forced structure from local freedom.

puzzles.title: The little boat
puzzles.instruction: Cover the boat, tip to tip.
puzzles.idea: A mirror can help us predict a matching move.
hints: Look at the two bottom corners.
Each bottom corner has just one neighbor.
Pair the bottom-left two and bottom-right two. Finish the top pair.

parent.notice: Notice whether your child finds matching moves on the two sides.
parent.prompt: If this side needs a domino, what might the other side need?
parent.explanation: Both bottom corners force horizontal pairs. The two top squares then pair with each other. Reflection preserves this single tiling.
parent.extension: Fold a paper drawing along the middle. Do the dominoes match across the fold?
parent.connection: Symmetry can simplify a constraint problem.

puzzles.title: Leave a friend
puzzles.instruction: Cover the picnic blanket.
puzzles.idea: Every square needs a neighbor at the end.
hints: Look ahead before placing a domino.
Try leaving two touching squares, not two far-apart ones.
A fresh start: cover each row with two dominoes across.

parent.notice: Treat undoing a move as useful information.
parent.prompt: If a square gets left alone, which earlier move could you change?
parent.explanation: Four horizontal dominoes work. Some legal partial placements can leave isolated squares. A legal next move does not always lead to a complete tiling.
parent.extension: Find a second complete tiling and compare just the part that changed.
parent.connection: Backtracking revises a local decision to meet a global condition.

puzzles.title: Around the pond
puzzles.instruction: Cover every square around the pond.
puzzles.idea: A first choice can guide a whole loop.
hints: The pond in the middle stays empty.
Choose a partner for one corner, then follow the edge.
Pair the top-left with the top-middle. Keep pairing around the pond.

parent.notice: Once one pair is chosen, the other pairs follow around the loop.
parent.prompt: Can you start the first domino the other way?
parent.explanation: The eight squares form a loop. Pairing neighbors in either alternating pattern gives its two tilings. There is no complete 2 by 2 square here to flip.
parent.extension: Try changing one ring tiling into the other. No sequence of two-domino flips can do it; several dominoes must be lifted together.
parent.connection: Holes can change which rearrangements are possible.

puzzles.title: Two cozy rooms
puzzles.instruction: Cover both little rooms.
puzzles.idea: Small solutions can fit together.
hints: Look for a square room at each end.
Each room can hold two dominoes.
Cover the top-left room across. Cover the bottom-right room across.

parent.notice: Look for the child grouping squares into useful chunks.
parent.prompt: Can you solve one room and reuse that idea in the other?
parent.explanation: The board separates into two 2 by 2 rooms along a vertical cut. Each has two tilings, giving four complete tilings. A domino across the single joining edge cannot complete the board: it would leave three squares in each room.
parent.extension: Keep one room fixed and find both choices for the other room.
parent.connection: Independent choices lead to multiplication when counting.

puzzles.title: The tiny crown
puzzles.instruction: Cover the whole crown.
puzzles.idea: Explain why your choices must work.
hints: Find the two side tips.
Each side tip has only one partner.
Cover each side tip with its neighbor. Finish the top pair and the bottom pair.

parent.notice: Invite an explanation in pointing and gestures, not just words.
parent.prompt: Can you show why no other domino can cover this tip?
parent.explanation: The left and right tips force the two middle-row horizontal pairs. The top and bottom pairs are then forced. Listing these reasons proves the tiling is unique.
parent.extension: Ask your child to teach someone else which pair must come first.
parent.connection: A chain of unavoidable choices is a small proof.

puzzles.title: The long greenhouse
puzzles.instruction: Cover the two-row greenhouse.
puzzles.idea: The first column gives two kinds of start.
hints: Focus on the two squares at the far left.
Cover them together, or send both dominoes to the right.
Five upright dominoes will cover the board.

parent.notice: Listen for a child separating cases rather than guessing every arrangement.
parent.prompt: What are the two ways the left edge can begin?
parent.explanation: Either the first column is one vertical domino, or its two squares begin two horizontal dominoes. Those choices leave a shorter two-row rectangle. This board has eight tilings.
parent.extension: Draw two-row boards of lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their counts are 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8. Explain the add-the-last-two rule.
parent.connection: A recurrence counts big objects by smaller cases.

puzzles.title: A hook with a room
puzzles.instruction: Cover the hook-shaped garden.
puzzles.idea: Find the part that cannot change.
hints: Look at the top-right tip.
Its only neighbor is the square just left of it.
Cover the rightmost top pair. Fill the remaining two-column rectangle.

parent.notice: A forced pair can make an irregular outline familiar.
parent.prompt: Which domino appears in every solution?
parent.explanation: The rightmost top pair is forced. Removing it leaves a 3 by 2 rectangle with three tilings, so the hook has three tilings as well.
parent.extension: Find all three by keeping the forced pair fixed.
parent.connection: Removing a forced edge reduces a matching problem.

puzzles.title: Odd-height orchard
puzzles.instruction: Cover the three-row orchard.
puzzles.idea: A useful split can ignore the outline.
hints: The board is three squares tall but four squares wide.
Rows of four can each make two pairs.
Place two horizontal dominoes in each row.

parent.notice: A tall odd side does not make the whole rectangle impossible.
parent.prompt: Why does pairing across the rows work?
parent.explanation: There are twelve squares, so every tiling uses six dominoes. Each row has an even length and can be tiled separately. Counting area is necessary, while an actual arrangement proves possibility.
parent.extension: Can you include two vertical dominoes? Turn the two dominoes in one 2 by 2 patch.
parent.connection: Constructive proofs give an arrangement, not only a count.

puzzles.title: The offset terraces
puzzles.instruction: Cover both terraces without gaps.
puzzles.idea: Choose a split that leaves solvable pieces.
hints: Look at the top two rows as one terrace.
The bottom two rows form another terrace, shifted right.
Use three vertical dominoes in the top terrace and three in the bottom terrace.

parent.notice: The child can choose an imaginary boundary through a connected board.
parent.prompt: Which two small rectangles can you see?
parent.explanation: Splitting between rows two and three gives two 2 by 3 rectangles. Tiling those separately proves the whole board works. Some other solutions cross the split; our construction need not find every solution.
parent.extension: Find a solution that does cross the middle split, then compare it with the two-terrace method.
parent.connection: Decomposition proves existence without claiming uniqueness.

puzzles.title: The connecting hallway
puzzles.instruction: Cover the two rooms and the hallway.
puzzles.idea: A narrow connection can force a domino.
hints: Look at the two middle hallway squares.
Try pairing those two squares with one another.
Then cover the left 2 by 2 room and the right 3 by 2 room.

parent.notice: Ask for a reason the hallway pair is needed.
parent.prompt: What would be left in the left room if a domino reached out of it?
parent.explanation: The left room has four squares and only one edge to the hallway. A crossing domino would leave three squares there, which cannot be paired internally. Thus the hallway squares pair together. The two rooms then offer 2 times 3 = 6 tilings.
parent.extension: Draw an imaginary line at each doorway. How many dominoes cross it in your solution?
parent.connection: Parity across a cut constrains a perfect matching.

puzzles.title: Missing corners
puzzles.instruction: Cover the garden with two corners missing.
puzzles.idea: Check both colors, then find a construction.
hints: The missing corners are at opposite ends of this three-row board.
Look for vertical pairs near the top-right and bottom-left corners.
Pair the top-right square downward, and the bottom-left square upward; complete the touching pairs.

parent.notice: Count squares of each checkerboard color if coloring is available.
parent.prompt: Why does every domino use one square of each color?
parent.explanation: On this 3 by 4 board, the two removed corners have opposite checkerboard colors. Five squares of each color remain. That check permits a tiling but does not prove one exists; completing the board provides the proof.
parent.extension: On paper, instead remove the two top corners of a 3 by 3 board. Those corners share a color, so the remaining odd number of squares cannot tile.
parent.connection: An invariant can rule out a possibility before searching.

puzzles.title: A tight entrance
puzzles.instruction: Cover the little entrance and the big room.
puzzles.idea: A small group needs enough possible partners.
hints: Start at the far-left tip.
After that pair is placed, the last entrance square needs a partner below.
Pair the first two top squares, then pair the third top square downward.

parent.notice: Watch how one forced pair reveals another.
parent.prompt: Which neighbor will this square still have after your first move?
parent.explanation: The far-left pair is forced. Then the third top square can only pair with the square below it. The remaining eight-square room has four tilings. Every complete solution shares the first two dominoes.
parent.extension: Before a move, point to a square whose last possible partner might disappear.
parent.connection: This is the local face of the matching bottleneck question.

puzzles.title: The small diamond
puzzles.instruction: Cover the diamond garden.
puzzles.idea: The border shapes the choices inside.
hints: Each row has an even number of squares.
Pair squares across to make a first solution.
Cover the top pair, both middle rows in pairs, and the bottom pair.

parent.notice: After one solution, ask where a small change is possible.
parent.prompt: Which two dominoes could turn together inside a square?
parent.explanation: This is an Aztec diamond of order two. Its twelve cells have eight tilings. The horizontal construction is one, and local 2 by 2 flips produce others.
parent.extension: Draw several solutions and mark which dominoes stay near the same boundary.
parent.connection: Larger Aztec diamonds reveal striking patterns in random tilings.

puzzles.title: Keep the leftovers friendly
puzzles.instruction: Cover the greenhouse and its lower room.
puzzles.idea: A good partial solution leaves a solvable remainder.
hints: Look for a small room at the bottom.
Cover that 2 by 2 room first if you like.
Then cover the upper two rows with five upright dominoes.

parent.notice: Praise a reason for undoing a move, not speed.
parent.prompt: What do you know about the shape left after your next domino?
parent.explanation: The lower four cells form a square and the upper ten form a two-row rectangle. Tiling those parts separately is a safe construction. Other legal starts may need revision.
parent.extension: Find a solution with a domino crossing from the top section to the lower room.
parent.connection: A search algorithm keeps decisions only when the remaining constraints allow completion.

puzzles.title: The square pond
puzzles.instruction: Cover the path around the square pond.
puzzles.idea: A hole changes the rearrangement game.
hints: Keep the four pond squares empty.
Start at a corner and follow the outside path.
Pair the top row across, the bottom row across, and the two middle squares of each side vertically.

parent.notice: There are two complete arrangements, but no two-domino square to turn.
parent.prompt: Can you change just two dominoes and still cover the board?
parent.explanation: The twelve cells make one cycle. Exactly two alternating pairings cover it. Neither contains a 2 by 2 patch, so neither allows a local flip.
parent.extension: Compare this board with the solid 4 by 4 board. The hole removes a way to rearrange tiles locally.
parent.connection: A tiling space can split into separate components.

puzzles.title: Three linked rooms
puzzles.instruction: Cover the three square rooms.
puzzles.idea: Repeated independent choices multiply.
hints: Find a 2 by 2 room at each step.
Cover each room on its own.
One solution uses a horizontal domino in every two-square row segment.

parent.notice: Keeping a chosen boundary helps organize all the solutions.
parent.prompt: If each room has two choices, how many choices do all three rooms have?
parent.explanation: Each 2 by 2 room has two tilings. A domino across either single joining edge would leave an odd number of cells on one side, so it cannot occur. The choices are independent: 2 times 2 times 2 gives eight tilings.
parent.extension: List the eight solutions with three symbols: across or upright for each room.
parent.connection: Product counting turns geometry into short symbolic descriptions.

puzzles.title: The rearranging courtyard
puzzles.instruction: Cover the courtyard. Then try a new pattern.
puzzles.idea: Solutions themselves can form a network.
hints: Start with a pattern you can repeat.
Two dominoes in a 2 by 2 square can turn together.
A first solution is two horizontal dominoes in each row.

parent.notice: Keep the puzzle goal simple; the rearrangement is an optional conversation.
parent.prompt: Can you make another solution by changing just two dominoes?
parent.explanation: There are 36 tilings of this 4 by 4 board. A local flip trades two parallel dominoes in a square for the other orientation. Recording tilings as dots and flips as links makes a new graph.
parent.extension: Draw three or four linked solutions. A theorem guarantees all tilings of a simply connected domino region are linked by such flips.
parent.connection: The move graph of tilings is a research object.

puzzles.title: The Fibonacci greenhouse
puzzles.instruction: Cover the greenhouse; look for smaller cases.
puzzles.idea: Count by the first choice, not by guessing.
hints: At the left edge, choose one vertical domino or two horizontal dominoes.
Those starts leave widths five and four.
Six vertical dominoes give a first complete tiling.

parent.notice: A reason for an exhaustive case split matters more than remembering a sequence.
parent.prompt: Why can no other kind of start occur at the left edge?
parent.explanation: Let T(n) count tilings of a two-row rectangle of width n. The first column is covered by one vertical domino or by two horizontals. Thus T(n)=T(n-1)+T(n-2), with T(0)=T(1)=1. This board has T(6)=13 tilings.
parent.extension: Predict T(7) without drawing all the solutions: 13+8=21. Explain why the two cases cannot overlap.
parent.connection: Recurrences and recursive algorithms turn geometry into enumeration.

puzzles.title: Two hooks, one plan
puzzles.instruction: Cover the hooks by finding small solvable parts.
puzzles.idea: Separate constraints from choices.
hints: Look at the far-right pair on the bottom row.
That bottom tip forces a horizontal domino.
After that pair, cover the top two rows across and the remaining left squares in pairs.

parent.notice: Ask which claims describe one strategy and which hold in every solution.
parent.prompt: Is this domino forced, or is it simply a useful choice?
parent.explanation: The bottom-right tip forces its neighbor. The remaining region can be tiled in several ways. The complete board has ten tilings, so a successful construction alone does not establish uniqueness.
parent.extension: Find one domino present in every tiling and one that can be changed.
parent.connection: Existence, uniqueness and counting are different questions.

puzzles.title: Odd rows, even width
puzzles.instruction: Cover the orchard with a plan you can explain.
puzzles.idea: Area is a necessary check; a tiling is a witness.
hints: There are eighteen squares.
Each row can be split into three neighboring pairs.
Place three horizontal dominoes in each of the three rows.

parent.notice: Encourage a statement that also applies to larger rectangles.
parent.prompt: Why can every rectangle with an even width be tiled this way?
parent.explanation: Pair consecutive cells in every row. This works for any rectangle with even width, regardless of height. Conversely, a rectangle with both side lengths odd has odd area and cannot be covered by two-cell tiles.
parent.extension: Now remove two opposite corners from a 4 by 4 paper board. There are fourteen squares, but the color counts differ, so area alone misses the obstruction.
parent.connection: Constructive arguments and invariants answer complementary questions.

puzzles.title: The sloping ridge
puzzles.instruction: Cover the ridge while protecting the narrow ends.
puzzles.idea: Global completion may force central choices.
hints: The top row and bottom row each form a pair.
Look for more forced pairs after the ends are covered.
A complete construction puts dominoes across each row, working left to right.

parent.notice: This board has fewer solutions than its size may suggest.
parent.prompt: Which choices disappear after you cover the two narrow ends?
parent.explanation: Every row has even length, so horizontal pairing provides a tiling. Exhaustive enumeration finds only four tilings: the narrow border forces many choices that look flexible at first.
parent.extension: Try to find the small patches where changes are actually possible. Compare a large rectangle with the same area.
parent.connection: Boundary conditions can strongly restrict a tiling space.

puzzles.title: A good place to split
puzzles.instruction: Cover the bent garden by choosing a useful split.
puzzles.idea: A decomposition is a proof strategy.
hints: The left part is a rectangle two rows tall and three columns wide.
The right part is a rectangle four rows tall and three columns wide.
Cover the left part vertically. Cover the right part in two-row strips.

parent.notice: The child chooses an imaginary boundary and explains why both sides work.
parent.prompt: Does your split find all solutions, or just enough to prove one exists?
parent.explanation: The two rectangles have six and twelve cells. Tiling them separately constructs a solution. A domino across the single joining edge would leave an odd number of cells on each side, so no complete tiling crosses it. The independent counts multiply: 3 times 11 gives 33.
parent.extension: Explain why a domino cannot cross this particular cut. Then compare the board with odd rooms and a forced crossing.
parent.connection: Divide-and-conquer can prove existence without enumerating everything.

puzzles.title: The color-balance garden
puzzles.instruction: Cover the garden with its two top corners removed.
puzzles.idea: A coloring test can reject a board, but cannot certify every board.
hints: There are twenty-two squares: eleven of each checkerboard color.
The shortened top row has four cells.
Cover each row horizontally, including the top row.

parent.notice: Separate the useful test from a complete proof.
parent.prompt: What does equal color balance tell us, and what does it not tell us?
parent.explanation: Each domino covers one square of each checkerboard color. These two removed corners have opposite colors, so balance remains. The horizontal row construction proves this particular board is tileable. Equal color counts alone are not sufficient for arbitrary shapes.
parent.extension: On a 4 by 4 paper board, remove opposite corners instead. Both missing squares have the same color, making domino tiling impossible.
parent.connection: Invariants give obstructions; matchings give actual solutions.

puzzles.title: The unavoidable bridge
puzzles.instruction: Cover both odd-sized rooms and their shared doorway.
puzzles.idea: An odd region must send a domino across its boundary.
hints: Each 3 by 3 room contains nine squares.
An odd room cannot be tiled entirely on its own.
Place a horizontal domino across the middle doorway, then tile each remaining eight-square room.

parent.notice: The bridge is forced even though neither of its cells is initially a tip.
parent.prompt: Why must a domino cross the doorway?
parent.explanation: Each room has odd area. The only adjacency between rooms is the middle doorway, so its crossing domino is forced. Removing it leaves two 3 by 3 boards missing a corner, each with four tilings; the full board has sixteen.
parent.extension: For any cut, the parity of the number of crossing dominoes equals the parity of the number of cells on one side. Prove it by counting the cells covered internally in pairs.
parent.connection: Cut constraints are a bridge from parity to perfect matching theory.

puzzles.title: The Aztec garden
puzzles.instruction: Cover the diamond; notice choices near its border.
puzzles.idea: The shape of a region influences its typical tilings.
hints: Every row contains an even number of cells.
Horizontal pairs give an easy first tiling.
Pair left to right in each row, starting with the two-cell top row.

parent.notice: This small board invites a question about large families, not a claim about statistics from one play.
parent.prompt: If we drew many different tilings, which patterns might keep appearing?
parent.explanation: This order-three Aztec diamond has 24 cells and 64 tilings, verified by enumeration. Every tiling uses twelve dominoes, but orientations and positions vary.
parent.extension: Sketch several tilings. Large uniformly random Aztec diamonds have a disordered central region approaching a circle and ordered outer regions. A hand-chosen sample here is not uniform and this tiny board is not the limiting theorem.
parent.connection: A small counting question leads to random tilings and limit shapes.

puzzles.title: The windowed courtyard
puzzles.instruction: Cover the courtyard around the little window.
puzzles.idea: A valid local move still needs a global check.
hints: The two missing squares form a window in the second row.
Each remaining row segment has even length.
Pair the top row across, both pairs beside the window across, then both bottom rows across.

parent.notice: Ask what remains possible after a move near the window.
parent.prompt: Can you explain why the squares left over still fit together?
parent.explanation: The row-by-row construction tiles all 22 cells. There are 75 complete tilings. The hole changes the available connections; merely preserving equal checkerboard counts after a placement does not guarantee completion.
parent.extension: Choose a square with few remaining neighbors before choosing a square with many. Explain why that may reveal trouble sooner.
parent.connection: Constraint propagation makes exact-cover search more efficient.

puzzles.title: The frozen ring
puzzles.instruction: Cover the narrow ring around the large pond.
puzzles.idea: Several solutions need not be linked by small flips.
hints: The sixteen cells form a single loop.
Once the first pair is chosen, keep alternating pairs around the loop.
Start with the two leftmost top cells; follow the perimeter to finish.

parent.notice: This board deliberately breaks an overgeneralization from solid rectangles.
parent.prompt: There are two tilings. Can a two-domino square flip connect them?
parent.explanation: The cycle has exactly two perfect matchings. Every domino choice forces the next around the ring. There is no 2 by 2 patch, so each solution has zero local flips. The two tilings occupy different components of the flip graph.
parent.extension: Compare with the solid courtyard. The theorem linking every pair by flips requires a simply connected region; this ring has a hole.
parent.connection: Topology can obstruct local transformations.

puzzles.title: A growing staircase
puzzles.instruction: Cover the staircase using a pattern that can grow.
puzzles.idea: Find a rule that works for a whole family.
hints: Count the squares in each row: 2, 4, 6, 4, 2.
Every count is even.
Pair each row from its left edge.

parent.notice: A repeatable argument is stronger than a single successful drawing.
parent.prompt: What property of every row makes your method work?
parent.explanation: Each row is one contiguous even-length interval. Pairing consecutive squares tiles it. Therefore any board whose rows are contiguous even-length intervals has this construction, regardless of how the rows are shifted.
parent.extension: On paper, explore a different tile: every 2^n by 2^n square with one cell removed can be tiled by L-trominoes. A central L gives each of four smaller squares one missing cell. Those three-cell tiles are not in this domino game.
parent.connection: A construction for an entire family prepares for induction.

puzzles.title: A whole world of tilings
puzzles.instruction: Cover the courtyard, then explore a small change.
puzzles.idea: Ask about all solutions and the paths between them.
hints: A repeated row pattern is a useful first solution.
Look for a full 2 by 2 patch covered by two dominoes.
Start with three horizontal dominoes in each row; a pair of neighboring rows contains places to flip.

parent.notice: Celebrate a new question after solving: how many, how connected, how typical?
parent.prompt: Could you reach every tiling by turning two dominoes at a time?
parent.explanation: This 4 by 6 rectangle has 281 tilings. A local flip exchanges the two tilings of a 2 by 2 patch. Because the board is simply connected, its tilings are connected by flips. A height function encodes the tiling as integer heights at grid vertices.
parent.extension: Draw a short path of flips. Advanced questions study shortest paths, efficient random sampling, and fluctuations of height functions on much larger boards; this MVP does not measure those quantities.
parent.connection: Thurston’s height viewpoint links local moves with global structure.

puzzles.title: Two little cups
puzzles.instruction: Swap the two cups. Put each cup on its matching spot.
puzzles.idea: A swap can undo itself.
hints: Find the spot for cup A.
Each cup will move to the other spot.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: Your child tracks both cups, not only the one they tap first.
parent.prompt: If we do the same swap again, where will the cups go?
parent.explanation: The two cups exchange places. Repeating that exact exchange returns to the starting arrangement; no cup disappears or changes its name.
parent.extension: Use two toys. Predict the result after two swaps, then three.
parent.connection: The first tiny example of an inverse: a transposition is its own inverse.

puzzles.title: One cup can rest
puzzles.instruction: One cup is home. Help the other two get home.
puzzles.idea: Notice what can stay the same.
hints: Which cup already matches its spot?
Look at the two cups that do not match.
From the start, try swapping spots 2 and 3.

parent.notice: They notice a cup that can be left alone.
parent.prompt: Which two cups need to trade places?
parent.explanation: A is already home. Swapping B and C solves the puzzle while preserving A. Looking for the part that is already correct reduces the work.
parent.extension: With three toys, make a new puzzle in which a different toy stays home.
parent.connection: A fixed point is an item a permutation leaves in place.

puzzles.title: Follow cup A
puzzles.instruction: Help all three cups find their spots.
puzzles.idea: One move can make the next move clear.
hints: Find cup A and its home.
Put A home, then look at the other two.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They follow one cup through a move and inspect what remains.
parent.prompt: After A gets home, who still needs to move?
parent.explanation: The cups make a three-cup cycle: each is sitting in another cup's home. Two swaps suffice. One cannot suffice because a swap touches only two spots, while all three begin wrong.
parent.extension: Make the same puzzle with toys. Can you solve it by helping B first?
parent.connection: Following where each item belongs is the concrete beginning of cycle decomposition.

puzzles.title: Around the other way
puzzles.instruction: The cups moved around. Bring them home.
puzzles.idea: A plan can work in more than one direction.
hints: Point from each cup to its home.
Choose one cup to put home first.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They reuse a strategy after the starting order changes.
parent.prompt: Does helping A first still work?
parent.explanation: This is the other three-cup cycle. A familiar plan still works: put one cup home, then exchange the remaining two. The visible letters change, but the structure of the task stays the same.
parent.extension: Ask the child to invent a three-cup scramble with nobody home.
parent.connection: The two directions of a three-cycle are inverse permutations.

puzzles.title: Two friendly pairs
puzzles.instruction: Two pairs traded places. Help both pairs get home.
puzzles.idea: Separate jobs can be done in either order.
hints: A and B can help each other.
Then look at C and D.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They see two small puzzles inside a bigger one.
parent.prompt: Could we help C and D before A and B?
parent.explanation: A and B need one exchange, and C and D need another. These swaps use different spots, so either order has the same result.
parent.extension: Do the two repairs in opposite orders with toys. Compare the endings.
parent.connection: Disjoint transpositions commute: independent operations can be reordered.

puzzles.title: Four-cup trail
puzzles.instruction: Put the four cups home, one step at a time.
puzzles.idea: A bigger cycle can be broken into smaller jobs.
hints: Start by finding cup A.
After one cup is home, help another cup.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They keep working after a move solves only part of the puzzle.
parent.prompt: Which cup could we settle next?
parent.explanation: All four cups belong to one cycle. Three well-chosen swaps solve it. Fixing a cup breaks a piece off the remaining cycle, so the same small strategy can be repeated.
parent.extension: Make a trail with five toys and try the same plan together.
parent.connection: This is an accessible instance of breaking a cycle into transpositions.

puzzles.title: Little stepping stones
puzzles.instruction: Only linked spots can swap. Help the cups home.
puzzles.idea: A cup can travel in small steps.
hints: Look at the links before you tap.
Cup C can travel toward its home one link at a time.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They distinguish a desired move from an allowed move.
parent.prompt: Can C jump straight home, or does it need a stop?
parent.explanation: C starts two links from home. Two neighbor swaps carry it across the row and also settle A and B. The route matters even when the goal stays the same.
parent.extension: Make a row of three paper spots and let toys move only between neighbors.
parent.connection: Neighbor swaps are the local operations used by elementary sorting algorithms.

puzzles.title: Make room in the middle
puzzles.instruction: The end cups want to trade. Use the links.
puzzles.idea: A helpful move may move a cup away from home.
hints: The end cups are not linked.
Let the middle cup move for a little while.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They accept a temporary mismatch as part of a plan.
parent.prompt: Can B help the others and come back home?
parent.explanation: The two end cups cannot exchange directly. B must leave its correct spot temporarily; three neighbor swaps restore it while exchanging A and C.
parent.extension: Replay the three moves backward. What happens?
parent.connection: Restricted token routing shows why counting correct spots is not always a reliable progress measure.

puzzles.title: A quiet last cup
puzzles.instruction: Use the links to get A, B, and C home.
puzzles.idea: Reuse a small solution inside a larger puzzle.
hints: Cup D is already home.
Move A toward the first spot, one link at a time.
From the start, try swapping spots 2 and 3.

parent.notice: They recognize the three-cup task despite the extra cup.
parent.prompt: Can we finish while D rests?
parent.explanation: Two neighbor swaps move A left through C and then B. D need not move. An extra object does not always make the part needing work larger.
parent.extension: Add a fifth toy already at home. Does the plan change?
parent.connection: Decomposing a problem into an active part and fixed points is a useful algorithmic habit.

puzzles.title: The long way round
puzzles.instruction: Help the end cups trade places along the links.
puzzles.idea: A route can need some temporary stops.
hints: The end cups cannot swap directly.
Move D toward the last spot, then help the other cups.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They make a multi-step plan without expecting every cup to stay settled.
parent.prompt: Who needs to move out of the way?
parent.explanation: A and D exchange ends using five neighbor swaps. B and C can return home afterward. One route moves D all the way right, then moves A left through the middle cups.
parent.extension: Keep this starting order for the next puzzle and compare its new link.
parent.connection: The permitted edges define a routing problem; the shortest route depends on that graph.

puzzles.title: A new shortcut
puzzles.instruction: There is a new link. Use it to help the cups home.
puzzles.idea: Changing a rule can change the best plan.
hints: Look for the link joining the two end spots.
Which cups need to trade places?
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 4.

parent.notice: They inspect the changed links instead of automatically repeating the old plan.
parent.prompt: What can we do now that we could not do before?
parent.explanation: The start matches the previous puzzle, but the end spots are now linked. One swap solves it. Comparing identical starts isolates what the extra route changes.
parent.extension: Draw a different extra link on a row of toy spots. Invent a puzzle that uses it.
parent.connection: Adding an edge can shorten a shortest path in the configuration graph.

puzzles.title: The helping spot
puzzles.instruction: Every swap uses spot 1. Help B and C trade places.
puzzles.idea: Borrow a spot, then put its cup back.
hints: B and C cannot swap directly.
Let A's spot help them pass.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They use a correct cup as a temporary helper and restore it.
parent.prompt: How can A help B and C, then return home?
parent.explanation: The links form a star centered at spot 1. Three swaps through this hub exchange B and C and restore A. D can stay home throughout.
parent.extension: Try another pair of outer cups with real toys and one central paper spot.
parent.connection: A restricted set of swaps can still generate every arrangement. A hub provides indirect exchanges.

puzzles.title: Across the table
puzzles.instruction: Any two spots can swap. Bring the cups home.
puzzles.idea: Check the rules before choosing a route.
hints: B is already home.
A and C can exchange directly.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 3.

parent.notice: They use a long exchange when it is allowed.
parent.prompt: Do the two cups have to be neighbors today?
parent.explanation: One swap exchanges A and C. An unrestricted swap can repair two far-apart positions at once. Keeping the move rule explicit will matter when paths are introduced.
parent.extension: With three toys, compare this rule with neighbor-only swaps.
parent.connection: Changing the generating swaps changes distances between the same permutations.

puzzles.title: Trace the loop
puzzles.instruction: Follow where each cup belongs, then bring them home.
puzzles.idea: Follow a cycle of destinations.
hints: D can stay where it is.
Trace A's home, then the home of the cup sitting there.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They describe the loop A, B, C rather than treating each mismatch separately.
parent.prompt: Which cups are all waiting for one another?
parent.explanation: A, B, and C form a three-cycle; D is fixed. Two swaps solve the cycle. At least two are necessary because a single swap cannot move all three misplaced cups.
parent.extension: Find a different first swap that still leads to a two-swap solution.
parent.connection: Cycle decomposition describes an arrangement by its independent loops.

puzzles.title: Jobs in either order
puzzles.instruction: Fix both mixed-up pairs. Pick which pair goes first.
puzzles.idea: Independent moves can trade order.
hints: Which cups want each other's spots?
Repair one pair, then the other pair.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They explain why one repair does not spoil the other.
parent.prompt: Will switching the order of our two swaps change the answer?
parent.explanation: The two disjoint pairs each need one swap. The repairs do not share a spot, so both orders work. Swaps that share a spot need not behave this way.
parent.extension: Try swaps 1–2 and 2–3 in both orders on three toys. Compare the results.
parent.connection: This is a concrete contrast between commuting and noncommuting operations.

puzzles.title: Five in a loop
puzzles.instruction: Put the five cups home. Try keeping each settled cup safe.
puzzles.idea: Repeat a useful step.
hints: Put one cup in its matching spot.
Keep that cup home while you work on the others.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They apply the same repair step to a shrinking problem.
parent.prompt: What smaller puzzle is left after the first repair?
parent.explanation: A five-cycle can be split by settling one cup at a time. Four swaps suffice. The final swap settles the last two cups together.
parent.extension: Predict how this strategy would work for six cups arranged in one loop.
parent.connection: The repeating strategy is a simple algorithm; cycle structure explains its length.

puzzles.title: Pairs that crossed
puzzles.instruction: Only neighbors can swap. Put the cups in order.
puzzles.idea: Count pairs that are in the wrong order.
hints: Look for a neighbor pair in the wrong order.
Swap a wrong-order pair, then check again.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They use the target order to choose a swap instead of guessing.
parent.prompt: Which pair is backward compared with A, B, C, D?
parent.explanation: The backward pairs are C–A, C–B, and D–B. Each must cross once. Three neighbor swaps solve the puzzle, and each helpful swap removes one backward pair.
parent.extension: Write the three backward pairs on paper and cross them out as they pass.
parent.connection: These backward pairs are inversions, the standard measure behind insertion sort.

puzzles.title: Everyone crossed
puzzles.instruction: The row is backward. Use neighbor swaps to untangle it.
puzzles.idea: A count can explain how much work is needed.
hints: Every pair is in the wrong order.
Move A left or D right, one neighbor at a time.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They organize the count instead of losing track of repeated pairs.
parent.prompt: How many other cups does D need to pass? What about C?
parent.explanation: D must pass three cups, C must pass two, and B must pass A. That is 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 crossings. Six helpful neighbor swaps achieve exactly those crossings.
parent.extension: Reverse three toys and compare its 2 + 1 crossings with this row's six.
parent.connection: The triangular-number pattern comes from counting all unordered pairs.

puzzles.title: One long journey
puzzles.instruction: Cup E is far from home. Swap along the row.
puzzles.idea: One moving cup can settle many others.
hints: A, B, C, and D are in the right order already.
Move E right across its next neighbor.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They distinguish being in the right relative order from being on the correct spot.
parent.prompt: What happens to the other cups each time E moves right?
parent.explanation: E passes four cups. Each exchange puts the other cup in its home, so four swaps finish. Although all five cups start misplaced, their relative order makes the task simple.
parent.extension: Place the last toy first in a longer row. Predict the number of neighbor swaps.
parent.connection: Inversion count captures useful structure that the number of misplaced cups misses.

puzzles.title: Two travelers
puzzles.instruction: The end cups must trade places. Use neighbor links.
puzzles.idea: A shared crossing can help two travelers.
hints: Move E toward the far end.
After E is home, move A toward the first spot.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They see why some cups must move even though they start home.
parent.prompt: When A and E cross each other, does that help one cup or both?
parent.explanation: E is before four smaller cups, and A is after B, C, and D as well. These seven backward pairs give a seven-swap solution. Counting A–E twice would overcount their shared crossing.
parent.extension: Compare two, three, four, and five spots with only the end cups exchanged.
parent.connection: Counting inversions provides a lower bound and a matching constructive solution.

puzzles.title: Close the loop
puzzles.instruction: The end spots are linked now. Bring the cups home.
puzzles.idea: A new edge can create a shortcut.
hints: This is the same start as the last puzzle.
Find the new link between the end spots.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 5.

parent.notice: They compare two rule sets while holding the starting arrangement fixed.
parent.prompt: Why did the same scramble become easier?
parent.explanation: Adding the end-to-end link turns the path into a ring. A and E can now exchange in one move; the middle cups need not move at all. The neighbor-row crossing count no longer measures the minimum.
parent.extension: Invent another scramble that becomes easier when the end link is added.
parent.connection: A shortest-path bound must match the allowed operations; changing the graph changes the metric.

puzzles.title: A hub for three
puzzles.instruction: Every swap uses spot 1. Send B, C, and D home.
puzzles.idea: Use a temporary holding place.
hints: The three outer cups cannot swap directly.
Move an outer cup into spot 1, then follow its destination.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They plan to restore A after borrowing its spot.
parent.prompt: Can one borrowed spot help all three outer cups?
parent.explanation: B, C, and D form a cycle around the hub. Bring one into spot 1, route the displaced cups through that spot, then return A. Four swaps suffice, compared with two if any pair could exchange.
parent.extension: Write down which cup visits the hub after each move.
parent.connection: Token swapping on a star is a small, tractable routing problem.

puzzles.title: Two hub deliveries
puzzles.instruction: Use spot 1 to repair both mixed-up pairs.
puzzles.idea: Reuse a small sequence as a tool.
hints: B and C need to trade; D and E need to trade.
Repair one pair through spot 1, then reuse the same pattern.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They treat three swaps as one reusable exchange routine.
parent.prompt: Can the plan for B and C also help D and E?
parent.explanation: Each outer pair can be exchanged with three hub swaps that restore A. Reusing that routine solves both pairs in six swaps. The reusable sequence matters more here than speed.
parent.extension: Describe the three-move routine without naming particular cups.
parent.connection: Building a compound operation from allowed generators is a basic group-theoretic and algorithmic idea.

puzzles.title: Choose a way around
puzzles.instruction: The cups can travel around the loop. Find a way home.
puzzles.idea: More than one route may be worth trying.
hints: Look at both directions around the loop.
Try a plan, and use Undo if you want to compare another.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They compare plans instead of assuming the first plan is the only one.
parent.prompt: Could a cup get home by going the other way?
parent.explanation: There are two directions around the ring. A shortest solution uses six swaps, verified by checking all 120 arrangements. A successful longer route is still a valid solution.
parent.extension: After solving, draw arrangements as dots and connect two when one swap joins them.
parent.connection: This configuration graph turns a manipulation puzzle into a shortest-path problem; random walks on such graphs lead to deeper probability questions.

puzzles.title: Break one loop
puzzles.instruction: Any two spots can swap. Untangle the four-cup loop.
puzzles.idea: Use structure to explain a short solution.
hints: Trace the chain of cups waiting for one another's spots.
Try fixing one cup while leaving the smaller loop to solve.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They explain their strategy in terms of the loop, not only a memorized sequence.
parent.prompt: How does the loop change when one cup reaches home?
parent.explanation: This arrangement has one cycle. A swap can increase the number of cycles by at most one, while the goal has four one-cup cycles. At least three swaps are needed, and three suffice.
parent.extension: Predict the minimum for one loop of five cups, then test it.
parent.connection: The unrestricted minimum is n minus the number of cycles, counting fixed points.

puzzles.title: Two different loops
puzzles.instruction: Find the two loops. Bring all five cups home.
puzzles.idea: Add the work in independent parts.
hints: A and B make one loop.
C, D, and E make another loop.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They partition the problem into a pair and a three-cycle.
parent.prompt: How many swaps does each loop need?
parent.explanation: The pair needs one swap and the three-cycle needs two. Together they need three. Since there are five cups and two cycles, the cycle-count lower bound is also three.
parent.extension: Interleave repairs of the two loops. Does the order matter when their spots are disjoint?
parent.connection: Cycle decomposition makes a global optimization problem additive when every pair may swap.

puzzles.title: Two three-cup teams
puzzles.instruction: Untangle both teams. Look for a plan you can reuse.
puzzles.idea: Repeated structure suggests a repeated method.
hints: The first three cups form a loop.
The last three cups need the same kind of repair.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They transfer a method between matching subproblems.
parent.prompt: What stays the same when the cup names change?
parent.explanation: There are two three-cycles, each requiring two unrestricted swaps. Four swaps solve the full arrangement. Relabeling the cups changes the story but preserves the mathematical structure.
parent.extension: Could this starting arrangement be solved in exactly five swaps? Every swap changes parity, so all solutions here have even length.
parent.connection: Cycle structure and permutation parity provide information about whole families of solutions.

puzzles.title: One loop, six cups
puzzles.instruction: Bring all six cups home. Try to explain your plan.
puzzles.idea: A lower bound can prove a plan is best.
hints: Everyone belongs to the same loop.
Each well-chosen swap can split off one settled cup.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They support a minimum claim with a reason, not just repeated attempts.
parent.prompt: Why would four swaps be too few?
parent.explanation: One cycle must become six cycles. Since a swap increases that count by at most one, at least five swaps are necessary. A five-swap plan meets the bound. Counting only six misplaced cups gives the weaker bound of three.
parent.extension: Compare six cups in one loop with the two three-cycles in the previous puzzle.
parent.connection: An invariant or bounded-change statistic can certify optimality.

puzzles.title: Count the crossings
puzzles.instruction: Only neighbors can swap. Find the backward pairs.
puzzles.idea: Measure progress with inversions.
hints: A backward pair appears in the opposite order from the goal.
Swap backward neighbors to remove one crossing at a time.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They count pairs that need to pass, including pairs that are not neighbors yet.
parent.prompt: Which four pairs are in the wrong order?
parent.explanation: The inverted pairs are C–A, C–B, E–B, and E–D. A neighbor swap changes only the relative order of its two cups, so four swaps are necessary. Swapping inverted neighbors achieves four.
parent.extension: Explain why swapping two neighbors already in order adds one inversion.
parent.connection: The inversion statistic proves the running cost of adjacent-exchange sorting.

puzzles.title: The backward parade
puzzles.instruction: Reverse the parade using neighbor swaps.
puzzles.idea: Every pair can contribute once.
hints: Every pair starts backward.
Count the pairs as 4 + 3 + 2 + 1.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They recognize a triangular number without double-counting pairs.
parent.prompt: Why does this row need ten crossings?
parent.explanation: All ten pairs of five cups are inverted. Every successful neighbor-only solution must reverse their order. Ten helpful swaps are enough, and no shorter plan can cross all ten pairs.
parent.extension: Predict the minimum for six cups in reverse order. The pair count is 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15.
parent.connection: This is the worst case for adjacent-swap sorting, with n(n−1)/2 inversions.

puzzles.title: Two groups pass
puzzles.instruction: Let A, B, C pass D, E, F using neighbor swaps.
puzzles.idea: Count crossings as a product.
hints: Each group is already in order inside itself.
Each cup in one group must pass every cup in the other.
From the start, try swapping spots 3 and 4.

parent.notice: They organize nine crossings into three groups of three.
parent.prompt: Why is the needed crossing count 3 times 3?
parent.explanation: The only inverted pairs have one cup from each block. There are 3 × 3 = 9 such pairs. Nine swaps suffice. There is no need to disturb the order within either block.
parent.extension: Predict the crossing count for a block of two passing a block of four.
parent.connection: Counting pairs across two sets is the multiplication principle in a sorting problem.

puzzles.title: Does a shortcut help?
puzzles.instruction: The ends are linked now. Find a route for every cup.
puzzles.idea: An extra choice does not always shorten a best plan.
hints: This is the same start as the previous puzzle.
Each cup is three links from home, whichever way it travels.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They test the idea that an extra edge must always help.
parent.prompt: Could this ring finish in fewer than nine swaps?
parent.explanation: Each of six cups starts three ring-edges from home: total distance 18. One swap moves two cups one edge each, reducing that total by at most two. At least nine swaps are required. The earlier nine-swap path plan still works, so the new link does not improve the minimum.
parent.extension: Find a different start where the new end link does help.
parent.connection: Graph-distance lower bounds can certify routing optimality even when inversion count no longer applies.

puzzles.title: Borrow the hub
puzzles.instruction: Every swap uses spot 1. Untangle the outer loop.
puzzles.idea: A correct item may need to move temporarily.
hints: A is home, but every legal move must use A's spot.
Bring an outer cup into the hub and follow the loop.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They plan a temporary disruption and include its repair.
parent.prompt: Why can we not insist that A stay home?
parent.explanation: The four outer cups form a cycle and have no direct links to one another. A must leave its home so the cycle can pass through the hub. Five swaps suffice; a rule forbidding all temporary mismatches would prevent any move.
parent.extension: Compare with unrestricted swaps, where the same outer cycle needs only three.
parent.connection: The child meets the failure of a naive 'never disturb correct tokens' rule. Research on trees studies much subtler failures, including correct leaves.

puzzles.title: A pair and a loop
puzzles.instruction: Use the hub to repair the outer pair and outer loop.
puzzles.idea: Combine reusable routing routines.
hints: B and C form a pair; D, E, and F form a loop.
Finish one group and restore the hub before the next.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They build a full solution from two smaller procedures.
parent.prompt: What does each routine promise about the hub when it ends?
parent.explanation: The outer pair can be repaired in three hub swaps and the outer three-cycle in four. Both routines restore A, so they compose into a seven-swap solution. Exhaustive search confirms that seven is minimal here.
parent.extension: Describe the routine for an outer cycle of k cups. It uses k + 1 hub swaps when the hub begins and ends correct.
parent.connection: Local procedures with clear input and output conditions are useful in constructive proofs and algorithms.

puzzles.title: Reverse around a ring
puzzles.instruction: Bring the backward cups home using the ring links.
puzzles.idea: Compare lower bounds instead of trusting just one.
hints: The end link lets A and F pass directly.
Try tracing short routes for all the cups, then compare plans.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They distinguish a plausible lower bound from an attainable solution.
parent.prompt: Can the best-looking route for each cup work for all cups together?
parent.explanation: The total ring distance is ten, so distance alone only proves a bound of five swaps. Exhaustive search finds that seven are needed. The reversed permutation is odd, so every valid solution length is odd; parity rules out six but cannot by itself rule out five.
parent.extension: Compare the seven-swap ring solution with the fifteen swaps required on a path. Try to explain the remaining gap between the distance bound and seven.
parent.connection: Competing routing demands make token swapping richer than moving each token along its own shortest path.

puzzles.title: Map the possibilities
puzzles.instruction: Plan a way home around the ring. Compare two routes.
puzzles.idea: Think about a whole space of arrangements.
hints: Which allowed swap would put a cup home?
If your plan gets tangled, undo a move and explore another branch.
From the start, try swapping spots 1 and 2.

parent.notice: They regard exploration as comparing routes through possible arrangements.
parent.prompt: How could we record all the arrangements without losing any?
parent.explanation: There are 6! = 720 arrangements. Connect two when a legal swap joins them. A shortest route for this start has five edges, checked by breadth-first search. The puzzle asks for a chosen route; choosing swaps at random is a separate experiment on the same graph.
parent.extension: With three physical cups, choose one of the three pairs uniformly at each turn. Record the first return after at least one swap. Repeating the experiment gives an average tending to six, not necessarily six each time.
parent.connection: For a uniformly chosen allowed edge on a fixed connected spot graph, the configuration walk has uniform stationary law. The mean positive return is n!, even though real swaps force period two. Mixing results require an aperiodic convention; Diaconis–Shahshahani allow a no-swap step with probability 1/n.

parent.explanation: Unfold a rectangle into mirror copies: the reflected trajectory becomes a straight ray through a rectangular lattice. families.title: Lantern Wires
rules: A board is a graph: lanterns are vertices and every drawn wire is a legal move.
Pressing a wire flips both endpoint states. It never moves a lantern.
The goal is the entire displayed ON/OFF pattern, including lamps required to stay OFF.
When a press budget is displayed, it is part of completion. Undo restores a press; every successful replay within the budget is accepted.
Every successful replay within the budget is accepted; the supplied replay is only a witness.
families.mathematics: Binary graph incidence: solve Ax = initial XOR target over F₂. A path changes only its endpoints; cycles change nothing. Every reachable target on a tree has a unique reduced edge set, while cycles create alternative solutions. Minimizing presses is the minimum-cardinality T-join problem for the mismatch vertices. This is a direct small case of combinatorial optimization, not a claim to teach its general algorithm.
families.prerequisites: Entry: distinguish bright/dark and follow a two-object change. Later: compare start and target, plan paths and cancellations, and count a budget up to six. Difficulty is relative within the family, not a grade ceiling.

families.title: Clockwork Gates
rules: Positions are labeled 0 through n−1 clockwise; jumping k adds k and wraps around.
A jump counts landing positions, not positions passed over.
In count mode, choose a positive activation count before running the animation. The accepted answer is the first positive count at which every target is met together.
In gear mode, choose one fixed jump for the entire run; success is the specified first positive return time.
Reset and revised predictions are unlimited. No timing skill, written argument, or hidden feedback is needed.
families.mathematics: Translation in a finite cyclic group: x ↦ x+k mod n. One orbit has period n/gcd(n,k), but every shift is reversible whether or not that orbit visits the whole ring. The final linked-clock instances are an authored extension to simultaneous congruences in a product of cyclic groups; the shared activation counter is one orbit in that product.
families.prerequisites: Entry: follow clockwise landings and count to four. Later: coordinate two or three repeating sequences, starting phases, and counts up to twenty-two. Multiplication, gcd, and congruence notation are optional strategies.

families.title: Mirror Couriers
rules: Start exactly at the bottom-left corner (0,0), initially moving right and up.
A vertical wall reverses the horizontal direction; a horizontal wall reverses the vertical direction. Crossing an old part of the path has no effect.
Stop at the FIRST corner reached after launch. A corner collision is terminal, not a bounce.
Count only non-corner wall reflections. Predictions are submitted before the path animation.
A direction is specified by positive integer rise/run: move run units right per rise units up before reflection. The controls show this as an aim arrow; it is not necessary to read fraction notation.
Design modes accept every permitted setting satisfying the exact corner and reflection count; reset and replay are unlimited.
families.mathematics: Unfold a rectangle into mirror copies: the reflected trajectory becomes a straight ray through a rectangular lattice. For slope 1 and reduced dimensions w=ga,h=gb, the first corner has horizontal side right iff b is odd and vertical side top iff a is odd, after a+b−2 bounces. Rational directions reduce to the same lattice problem after scaling the axes. This is the elementary unfolding construction used in billiard dynamics and the torus model, without claiming ergodicity or density results.
families.prerequisites: Entry: follow a diagonal and distinguish a wall from a corner; no independent reading required. Later: count grid dimensions, compare repeated wall intervals, distinguish first arrival from a later one. Aiming levels require interpreting a rise/run arrow; fraction notation and gcd are optional strategies. The final level suits children comfortable coordinating two ratios, often 4–5 or beyond.

families.title: Bridge Courier
rules: Move along drawn roads without teleporting. Dots are junctions; crossings without dots are not junctions. Revisit dots freely. When the goal says exactly once, use each road once. For a distance target, cover every road, return to the marked depot, and meet the target; repeats are allowed. All roads are undirected. Every unlabelled road has length 1.
families.mathematics: Euler trails, degree parity, cycle splicing, bridges, and the undirected route-inspection (Chinese postman) problem. The change from exact-once to shortest delivery explicitly introduces necessary repetition. Pairing odd vertices explains the optimization; no proof answer is required.
families.prerequisites: No reading with narration; track five used edges.

families.title: Symbol Orchard
rules: Fill each empty cell with one of the displayed symbols. Every row and every column must contain each symbol exactly once. Keep given cells fixed. No boxes, diagonals, visibility counts, or extra rules. Symbols 1–n may be displayed as distinct fruit shapes; their arithmetic values do not matter.
families.mathematics: Latin squares, partial Latin-square completion, quasigroup multiplication tables, and determining sets. The same uniform row/column condition defines the entire object; fixed entries reveal part of that object. Later puzzles expose the gap between local consistency and global completion.
families.prerequisites: Match two symbols; follow a row and a column. No arithmetic or independent reading.

families.title: Signal Lanterns
rules: Each position is 0 or 1 (display as two labeled shapes/colors); repetitions are allowed. A recorded test earns one match for each symbol in the correct position. Only the total is shown: no indication of which positions match and no right-symbol/wrong-position score. All tests are visible from the start. Set the secret code that fits every test, then submit; there is no query budget or proof requirement.
families.mathematics: A secret is a vertex of a binary hypercube. Its match score is length minus Hamming distance to a test vertex. Decoding intersects distance shells. Instances 05 and 06 use a resolving set for all 32 five-bit words. Later transcripts need only identify their authored secret uniquely; they do not claim to resolve every possible word.
families.prerequisites: Match positions and distinguish two symbols; count zero.

families.title: Pebble Duel
rules: Two players alternate. On a turn, remove any positive number of counters from exactly one pile; removing the whole pile is allowed. Take the last counter to win (normal play). Empty piles remain labeled but cannot be chosen. The app takes a winning move whenever one exists, otherwise a random legal move.
families.mathematics: Normal-play impartial games and backward induction lead from equal two-pile positions to Nim sum zero. Binary column parity is addition over the field with two elements; this is Bouton’s classical solved game and an entry to Sprague–Grundy theory.
families.prerequisites: Count and remove 1 or 2; understand alternating turns.

families.title: Neighbor Lanterns
rules: Color every dot with the supplied palette. The endpoints of every drawn link must have different colors. Recolor freely; no fixed clues, color quotas, or one-off restrictions. A crossing without a dot is not a junction. Color dots, not links.
families.mathematics: Proper vertex coloring and chromatic number; bipartition, odd-cycle closure, wheels, graph powers, and the Petersen graph. The supplied palette is minimal, checked exhaustively. The player only has to produce a coloring, never a proof of minimality.
families.prerequisites: Distinguish two colors or shape patterns; no reading or counting.

families.title: Spring-water Jugs
rules: A fill goes to capacity; emptying removes all water; a pour continues until the source is empty or the destination is full. No stopping partway. Fill and Empty controls are available only when a spring and drain are provided. Otherwise the supply is sealed: pour only and keep every drop. All goal-reaching paths count; minima are optional replay targets.
families.mathematics: Integer state graphs, conserved quantities, gcd and integer linear combinations; Bézout reachability with a source/drain. The closed three-jug variant adds total-volume conservation; do not transfer the two-jug sufficiency theorem without checking.
families.prerequisites: Entry: count to 3; recognize full and empty.

families.title: Odd-pebble Balance
rules: Exactly one suspect pebble differs; all other pebbles have the same weight. Compare disjoint equal-size groups. A weighing reports left heavier, right heavier, or balance. The budget counts actual weighings. Declare only when the evidence uniquely identifies the pebble and, when required, whether it is heavy or light. A pebble marked Normal is a known genuine reference.
families.mathematics: Ternary decision trees, worst-case experimental design, information bounds, and signed hypotheses. A strategy must work on every consistent hidden state, not merely guess the chosen secret.
families.prerequisites: Entry: distinguish a tilt from balance.
